title: WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN WRONG ABOUT WHO GOD CHOOSES TO SAVE?
paragraphs: WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN WRONG ABOUT WHO GOD CHOOSES TO SAVE?

If God already knows who will enter heaven, does your decision to follow Jesus really matter? The answer reaches deeper than predestination, free will, and centuries of theological debate. It reaches into the heart of a God who saves sinners—and the soul of someone wondering whether there is still hope.
There is a question that has kept theologians awake for centuries.
But somewhere tonight, it is keeping an ordinary person awake for a very different reason.
Not because they are studying Greek.
Not because they are preparing a sermon.
But because they are lying in bed, staring at the ceiling, remembering everything they have done wrong.
The lies. The secret sins. The promises to God they broke. The prayers they stopped praying because they felt too ashamed to speak.
And somewhere between the silence and the regret, a frightening thought enters their mind.
What if God never chose me?
What if salvation has already been decided?
What if I want to come back to Jesus, but I am not one of the people He intends to save?
And on the other side of the question stands another person.
Someone who believes they can come to Christ whenever they want.
Tomorrow.
Next Sunday.
After one more relationship.
After one more season of living however they please.
They assume the door of mercy will always be waiting.
Two people.
Two very different fears.
One wonders whether the door was ever open.
The other assumes it can never close.
And both desperately need to hear what Scripture actually says.
Because this is not merely an argument about Calvinism and Arminianism.
This is about the character of God.
The condition of the human heart.
The meaning of the cross.
And whether the words of Jesus still reach the person who thinks they have wandered too far.
Listen carefully.
The Bible teaches that God is sovereign in salvation. It also calls human beings to repent, believe, and respond to the Gospel.
The difficult question is not whether Scripture teaches these truths.
It does.
The question is how they fit together.
And before we attempt to answer, we need to leave our pride at the door.
Because if we approach this subject determined to defend our theological camp more fiercely than we defend the truth of Scripture, we may win an argument while missing the beauty of Christ.
Imagine standing outside a courtroom.
You know the charges against you.
Not rumors.
Not exaggerations.
Actual sins.
You remember the moments when you knew what was right and deliberately chose what was wrong.
And then someone announces that the Judge has made a way for guilty people to be forgiven.
You ask, trembling, "Is that mercy really available to someone like me?"
That is where this conversation belongs.
Not merely in the classroom.
But at the foot of the cross.
Jesus said something in John 6:44 that should make every self-confident heart tremble:
"No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day." (KJV)
The original Greek begins with a striking declaration:

Οὐδεὶς δύναται ἐλθεῖν πρός με
Oudeis dynatai elthein pros me.
"No one is able to come to me."
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not merely say that people find coming to Him difficult.
He said no one is able to come unless the Father draws that person.
The Greek verb ἑλκύσῃ (helkysē), translated "draw," comes from helkō, a verb that can describe drawing or pulling.
But the word alone does not settle every theological question about whether this drawing can be resisted. Its meaning must be understood within the passage and the wider teaching of Scripture.
What is unmistakable is this:
Salvation does not begin with human beings independently climbing their way toward God.
God must act.
Grace is not heaven applauding our spiritual achievements.
Grace is God's undeserved kindness reaching people who cannot rescue themselves.
Paul writes in Ephesians 2:8–9:
The Greek word for grace is χάρις (charis).
It speaks of favor freely given, not wages earned.
And the Greek word for gift in this passage, δῶρον (dōron), reinforces the point that salvation is God's gift rather than the product of human merit.

The passage does not, by its grammar alone, settle every dispute about the relationship between faith and regeneration. But it leaves no room for anyone to boast that they purchased salvation through their own goodness.
Think about that.
The Christian does not stand before heaven saying, "I was intelligent enough to save myself."
The Christian says, "Jesus Christ had mercy on me."
And that changes everything.
But now comes the question that cannot be ignored.
If no one comes unless the Father draws them, does God draw everyone in the same way?
Does He choose particular people to save?
And if He does, what becomes of the invitation to the world?
Paul brings us directly into this mystery in Ephesians 1:4–5:

"According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love: Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will." (KJV)
The Greek word translated "chosen" is ἐξελέξατο (exelexato), from eklegomai, meaning to choose or select.
The word translated "predestinated" is προορίσας (proorisas), from proorizō, meaning to determine or appoint beforehand.
These are not imaginary concepts invented by theologians.
They are biblical words.
God's choosing is real.
His purpose is real.
His initiative in salvation is real.
But notice something precious that people sometimes rush past.
Paul says God chose believers "in him."
In Christ.
Not apart from Christ.
Not through some alternate doorway.
Not through a salvation that makes the cross unnecessary.
The center of God's saving purpose is Jesus Christ.
And when Paul describes the result, he does not portray a cold, impersonal selection process.
He speaks of adoption.
Children being brought into a family.
People who once stood outside being welcomed home.
The mystery of election is presented within the astonishing mercy of God in Christ.
Yet Christians who sincerely believe the Bible have disagreed about how this election relates to individual faith.

In the Reformed or Calvinist understanding, God's gracious election of particular sinners is not based on His foreseeing that they would independently choose Him. God effectively calls and brings His elect to faith in Christ.

In the classical Arminian understanding, God's grace comes first and enables sinners to respond, but that grace can be resisted. Election is commonly understood in relation to God's foreknowledge of faith in Christ, with important distinctions among Arminian theologians.
Other Christian traditions explain the relationship differently.
These differences are serious.
They cannot all be made identical simply by saying everyone agrees.
But neither should we pretend that every Christian who interprets these passages differently is rejecting Jesus.
The proper question is not, "Which theological label makes me feel safest?"
It is, "What does the whole counsel of God actually teach?"
And the whole counsel of God brings us to another astonishing declaration.
First Timothy 2:3–4 describes:
"God our Saviour; Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth." (KJV)
The Greek says:

πάντας ἀνθρώπους θέλει σωθῆναι
pantas anthrōpous thelei sōthēnai.
"[He] desires all people to be saved."
The word πάντας (pantas) means "all," while ἀνθρώπους (anthrōpous) refers to human beings or people.
Here, too, context matters.

Some interpreters understand "all people" as every individual without exception. Others understand the passage to emphasize all kinds or classes of people, especially because Paul has just urged prayer for everyone, including rulers and those in authority.
The Greek wording itself does not remove the need for careful interpretation.
But whatever position we take, we must not erase the Bible's testimony to God's goodness, His mercy, and His command that the Gospel be proclaimed.
Second Peter 3:9 declares that the Lord is:
"not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance." (KJV)
Christians debate how the word "any" relates to the people addressed in that passage and how God's stated desire relates to His eternal purposes.
But no faithful reading should turn this verse into an excuse for indifference toward the lost.
God is not indifferent to repentance.
Neither should we be.
And then we come to one of the most heartbreaking moments in the ministry of Jesus.
He looks toward Jerusalem.
A city with a long history of resisting God's messengers.
A city filled with religious activity, yet marked by stubborn unbelief.
And Jesus says:

"O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!" (Matthew 23:37, KJV)
Read those final words again.
"And ye would not!"
There is grief in this passage.
There is resistance.
There is the tragedy of people refusing the One who stands before them.
Jesus does not describe their rebellion as harmless.
He laments it.
The passage does not, by itself, settle the entire debate about irresistible grace or the precise relationship between Jerusalem's leaders and its inhabitants.
But it plainly reveals the seriousness of rejecting God's messengers and resisting the call of Christ.
And perhaps this is where the question begins to move from theology into your own life.
Because you may not know how to explain every dimension of divine sovereignty.
But you know what it feels like to resist conviction.
You know what it is to hear a sermon and feel as though every word has found the one room in your heart you keep locked.
You know what it is to whisper, "Lord, I know," and then continue doing what you know is destroying you.
You have felt the weight of an apology you refused to make.
The bitterness you defended.
The temptation you entertained.
The compromise you renamed so you would not have to repent.
And somewhere along the way, you may have begun using theological questions to avoid a deeply personal one.
What are you doing with Jesus Christ?
Not what is your denomination.
Not which preacher do you follow.
Not which argument can you win in a comment section.
What are you doing with the Son of God who calls sinners to repentance?
Because the Bible does not allow us to hide behind God's sovereignty as an excuse for unbelief.
Acts 17:30 declares that God:
"commandeth all men every where to repent." (KJV)
The Greek word commonly translated "repent" is μετανοέω (metanoeō).
It refers to a change of mind or understanding and, in biblical calls to repentance, involves turning from sin toward God.
Repentance is not merely feeling embarrassed because someone discovered your secret.
It is not crying during worship and returning unchanged to the same cherished rebellion.
And it is not becoming morally perfect before you dare approach Jesus.
Repentance means turning toward God with an honest acknowledgment of sin, abandoning the claim that your sin deserves to remain on the throne.
It is inseparable from the Gospel call to faith.
Jesus Himself proclaimed:
"The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel." (Mark 1:15, KJV)
In Greek, the commands are:

μετανοεῖτε καὶ πιστεύετε ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ
metanoeite kai pisteuete en tō euangeliō.
"Repent and believe in the Gospel."
There is no invitation here to purchase salvation.
There is no suggestion that repentance earns God's love.
There is a command to turn and trust the good news of Jesus Christ.
And what is that good news?
That the eternal Son of God came into the world.
That He lived without sin.
That He died for sinners.
That He was buried.
That He rose again on the third day.
That forgiveness and reconciliation with God are found through Him.
That the cross is not a decoration for religious people but the place where the seriousness of sin and the wonder of divine mercy meet.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we cleaned every stain.
Not after we proved ourselves worthy.
Not after we became the people our families wanted us to be.
While we were still sinners.
That does not mean God approves of sin.
It means His saving love is not a reward for our perfection.
The cross exposes sin precisely because sin is so serious that reconciliation required the saving work of Christ.
And the cross reveals grace precisely because Christ willingly gave Himself for those who could never earn that mercy.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Think of the apostle Paul.
Before he became a missionary, he persecuted the church.
He was not simply confused about a minor doctrine.
He was actively opposing followers of Jesus.
Acts 9 records him traveling toward Damascus with authority to arrest believers.
Then the risen Christ confronted him.
"Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" (Acts 9:4, KJV)
Imagine that moment.
The man convinced he was defending God discovered he was fighting against the Messiah.
Everything he had built his confidence upon was suddenly exposed.
His religious reputation could not save him.
His zeal could not justify him.
His knowledge could not erase his guilt.
And yet the Lord who confronted him would also transform him.
Paul later wrote:
"Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief." (1 Timothy 1:15, KJV)
He did not erase his past to make his testimony more impressive.
He remembered what mercy had rescued him from.
And then he declared that his experience displayed the patience of Christ toward those who would afterward believe.
The persecutor became a preacher.
The enemy of the church became a servant of the Gospel.
The man who once tried to silence the name of Jesus spent his life proclaiming it.
Not because sin was insignificant.
But because grace was greater than his guilt.
Now ask yourself something.
If you had met Saul before Damascus, would you have expected him to become an apostle?
Probably not.
You might have prayed for protection from him.
You might have feared his arrival.
You might have thought his heart was beyond reach.
But the story was not finished.
Never confuse someone's present rebellion with the final chapter of their life.
That includes the person you have almost stopped praying for.
The son who has walked away from church.
The daughter who seems angry at everything connected to God.
The husband who mocks your faith.
The friend who once worshiped beside you but now says they no longer believe.
And yes.
It includes you.
But Paul's conversion also raises the question again.
Was Saul chosen by God?
Clearly, God acted powerfully in his calling.
Did Saul respond?
Yes. His life was transformed in faith and obedience.
Yet the narrative of Saul's extraordinary calling does not automatically answer every question about the precise order of regeneration and faith for every believer.
We should not demand that one conversion account carry more doctrinal weight than it was written to bear.
Instead, we should let it show us what it unmistakably reveals.
Jesus Christ is powerful enough to save an enemy.
And His grace is capable of rewriting a life no human being could have predicted.
But someone will ask:
"If God chooses who will be saved, why evangelize?"
That question sounds reasonable until we remember that Scripture never separates God's saving purposes from His command to proclaim the Gospel.
Romans 10:13 says:
"For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved." (KJV)
Then Paul asks how people can call on One in whom they have not believed, and how they can believe without hearing.
God commands the message to be preached.
People are called to hear.
To repent.
To believe.
To call upon the Lord.
The Gospel is not a secret invitation reserved for people who can somehow discover whether their names appear in an unseen heavenly register.
The Gospel is to be proclaimed openly.
Jesus commanded His followers to make disciples of all nations.
We do not know the hidden purposes of God.
We have been given His revealed command.
And that command is not to speculate about who might be saved.
It is to preach Christ.
To love our neighbors.
To pray for the lost.
To tell the truth.
To bear witness to the resurrection.
And to invite people to repent and believe.
Some Christians understand that preaching as the means through which God effectually calls His elect.
Others understand it as the means through which God graciously enables people to respond in faith.
But both have a compelling reason to share the Gospel.
Because Christ commanded it.
And because people need to hear about Him.
Now consider the opposite question.
"If every person can respond, does that mean human beings save themselves by making the right decision?"
No.
That conclusion misunderstands grace.
Even theological traditions that strongly affirm a resistible human response generally insist that salvation is impossible without God's preceding grace.
A person who receives a gift does not thereby become the person who purchased it.
And a sinner who trusts Christ does not become the author of Christ's atoning work.
The disagreement is not whether grace is necessary.
Historic orthodox Christian teaching insists that it is.
The disagreement concerns how God's grace brings about faith and whether that saving grace can finally be resisted.
We must describe those differences accurately.
Because caricaturing another believer's position is not the same as refuting it.
And humility is not weakness when we are handling the Word of God.
Now we arrive at a passage that should speak directly to anyone afraid they are excluded from mercy.
Jesus says in John 6:37:
"All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out." (KJV)
Do you see the two declarations standing together?
The Father gives.
And the one who comes is not cast out.
Divine initiative.
A genuine promise to the person who comes.
Jesus does not say, "Come to Me, and I might reject you because you have asked too many questions."
He does not say, "Come to Me, but first prove that you were predestined."
He does not say, "Come to Me, provided your past is not too scandalous."
He says:
"Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out."
The Greek phrase is especially emphatic:

οὐ μὴ ἐκβάλω ἔξω
ou mē ekbalō exō.
"I will certainly not cast out."
The combination οὐ μή (ou mē) expresses a strong negation.
Christ is not speaking reluctantly.
He is giving a promise.
If you are coming to Jesus in repentance and faith, you do not need to solve every mystery of predestination before trusting His word.
You can take Him at His promise.
And perhaps that is the sentence you needed more than another theological argument.
Because you have spent so much time asking whether God could possibly want someone like you that you have almost stopped listening to what Jesus actually says.
Come.
Not because your sin is small.
Not because your record is clean.
Not because you understand every doctrine.
Come because Christ is the Savior of sinners.
Come with your guilt exposed.
Come with your excuses surrendered.
Come believing that His death and resurrection are sufficient to save.
And do not confuse coming to Christ with bargaining with Him.
You cannot negotiate your way into forgiveness.
You cannot purchase a new heart through religious performance.
You cannot compensate for rebellion by doing enough good deeds.
Salvation is not for sale.
It is found in Jesus Christ.
And this matters especially in a world where spiritual language is sometimes used to place financial pressure on wounded people.
But no donation can make God choose you.
No offering can purchase forgiveness.
The blood of Christ cannot be replaced by a transaction.
Acts 8:18–23 warns us through the account of Simon, who attempted to obtain spiritual power with money.
Peter rebuked him sharply.
God's gift is not merchandise.
Because the Gospel is worth more than any ministry platform.
And Jesus must remain greater than the organization proclaiming His name.
But there is another danger we must confront.
The person who says, "If God wants to save me, He will save me, so I can continue living however I please."
Friend, that is not biblical trust.
That is presumption.
The Bible never presents God's sovereignty as permission to cherish sin.
Paul asks in Romans 6:1–2:
"Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid." (KJV)
Grace does not give us a license to remain enslaved.
Grace brings us into a new relationship with Christ.
The person justified by faith is also called into a life of holiness, repentance, and growing obedience.
Not perfect performance.
Not sinless self-sufficiency.
But a real transformation through the work of God.
And that transformation may involve tears.
Confession.
Making restitution where appropriate.
Walking away from destructive habits.
Seeking help.
Rebuilding trust.
Learning to forgive.
Returning to Scripture after months of silence.
Beginning again after another painful failure.
Some changes happen dramatically.
Others unfold through years of sanctification.
But Jesus does not merely offer a religious label to place over an unchanged life.
He calls us to follow Him.
That is why this question matters so deeply.
Does God choose?
Scripture says He chooses.
Must people respond?
Scripture commands them to repent and believe.
Does salvation depend on human merit?
Absolutely not.
Is God's grace necessary?
Entirely.
Can we fully explain the relationship between God's eternal purposes and human responsibility in a way that resolves every theological disagreement?
Christians have wrestled with these questions for centuries, and Scripture should make us cautious about claiming more certainty than its words establish.
But there is something we can say without hesitation.
No sinner should use the mystery of election as a reason to refuse the clear invitation of Christ.
And no believer should use the doctrine of grace as a reason to become proud.
If you believe God sovereignly chose you, that should make you humble.
If you believe God graciously enabled you to respond, that should make you grateful.
Neither understanding gives you permission to look down on people who are struggling.
Neither makes you the Savior.
Jesus is the Savior.
And while Christians debate the order and operation of grace, the world is filled with people who have never understood the Gospel.
People who think Christianity is merely a system of rules.
People who assume God only welcomes those who have always lived respectably.
People who believe their failures have permanently disqualified them.
People who have been wounded by religious hypocrisy and now struggle to distinguish the failures of Christians from the character of Christ.
They need more than our theological pride.
They need the truth.
They need to hear that God is holy.
That sin is real.
That judgment is serious.
That Jesus died and rose again.
That repentance and faith are not optional decorations added to Christianity.
And that forgiveness is found in Him.
Perhaps someone reading this has been waiting for a sign.
Not a supernatural spectacle.
Just some assurance that the invitation of Jesus is not a cruel joke.
Hear His words again.
"Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out."
You do not have to look behind the curtain of eternity.
You are being called to look to Christ.
And there is another scene I want you to remember.
A thief hangs beside Jesus at Calvary.
He has no opportunity to rebuild his reputation.
No years left to demonstrate public moral improvement.
No chance to establish a ministry.
No impressive spiritual résumé to present.
His life is ending.
And he knows he deserves condemnation.
Yet he turns to Jesus and says:
"Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom." (Luke 23:42, KJV)
Jesus answers:
"Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise." (Luke 23:43, KJV)
That man could not earn his way down from the cross.
He could not repair the years he had wasted.
He could not undo the crimes that brought him there.
But he could turn to the crucified King in faith.
And Jesus received him.
The thief did not understand every mystery of divine election.
He knew he was guilty.
He knew Jesus was King.
And he entrusted himself to Him.
Do not misunderstand the lesson.
The thief's salvation does not make repentance unnecessary.
His words and acknowledgment of guilt reveal a remarkable change in his response to Jesus.
And his story does not give anyone permission to postpone repentance until the last moment.
One thief was saved at the cross.
The other is not recorded as receiving the same promise.
You do not know how much time remains.
You do not know whether tomorrow will bring another opportunity.
But you do know what Scripture calls you to do today.
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
And if you already belong to Him, stop treating the salvation of others like an abstract debate.
Pray for the person who hurt you.
Speak to the family member who has drifted away.
Share the Gospel with the friend who thinks their life is beyond repair.
Not because you can force someone into the kingdom.
You cannot.
But because the message of Jesus Christ is worth proclaiming.
And because you do not know what God may do through one conversation, one prayer, or one Scripture shared at the right moment.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to sell salvation.
Not to make people dependent on a personality or a platform.
But to keep pointing hearts back to the Word of God and the redeeming work of Jesus Christ.
These resources are meant to help people study Scripture, strengthen their faith, confront spiritual complacency, and continue growing beyond the momentary emotion of a single article.
And if this message has helped you, there are meaningful ways to help it reach others.
Not merely to increase a number.
Someone may have spent years believing they are too sinful to be forgiven.
Someone may be postponing repentance because they assume they have unlimited time.
Someone may need to read John 6:37 today.
And if someone comes to mind who is struggling privately, consider sending it to them personally with compassion rather than publicly exposing their pain.
Because they sometimes do.
Even mature Christians have moments when the mystery feels overwhelming.
And when that happens, you may need to return to the simple promise of Christ.
The One who comes to Him will not be cast out.
Give freely, not under pressure.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be done grudgingly or out of compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
You glorify Him through faith in Christ and a life shaped by His grace, including the many ways you love, serve, give, and bear witness to the truth.
That benefit is simply a gesture of appreciation.
The greater purpose is the Gospel.
The greater mission is discipleship.
And the greatest treasure is Jesus Christ.
I want to ask you something that may be harder to answer.
Are you using the mystery of God's choosing to avoid making an honest response to Jesus?
Maybe you have been telling yourself that you need to understand predestination before you can surrender.
Maybe you have been using your religious knowledge to avoid confronting your private sins.
Maybe you have spent so much time arguing about the freedom of the human will that you have neglected the freedom from sin that Christ came to bring.
Or perhaps you have been frightened that God would never receive you.
If that is you, do not let the fear of being rejected silence the invitation Jesus has actually given.
Come to Him.
Confess your sin.
Trust His finished work.
And keep seeking to know Him through Scripture, prayer, and fellowship with faithful believers.
If you have experienced God's mercy after years of wandering, share a testimony of what Christ has done in your life.
And if you disagree with a theological interpretation presented here, you are welcome to explain your understanding respectfully, with Scripture.
Let this be a place where people can ask difficult questions without being humiliated.
Where conviction leads toward repentance rather than despair.
Where testimony points toward Jesus rather than self-glory.
And where we remember that a wounded soul is more important than winning an argument.
You do not owe anyone your private confession in a public comment section. You can speak to God in the quiet of your room, and you can seek prayer privately from a trusted Christian.
But do not ignore the call of Christ.
Because the final answer to your deepest need is not a theological system.
It is not a famous preacher.
It is not a church tradition.
And it is certainly not a social media platform.
It is Jesus Christ.
The crucified and risen Lord.
The One who said, "Repent, and believe the gospel."
The One who said, "Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out."
The One whose mercy received a dying thief.
The One whose grace transformed a persecutor.
The One whose Gospel is still proclaimed to sinners today.
And maybe the most unforgettable truth in this entire conversation is not that we have managed to explain every mystery about God's eternal purposes.
It is that the Savior has spoken clearly enough for a sinner to know where to turn.
To Him.
Not to your record.
Not to your reputation.
Not to your ability to understand eternity.
To Jesus.
So when the question comes again—
"Does God choose who will be saved, or does every person have the freedom to respond?"
—remember the truths Scripture places before us.
God is sovereign.
Grace is necessary.
Human beings are commanded to repent and believe.
Salvation is through Jesus Christ, not human achievement.
And those who come to Him are not cast out.
We should continue studying the passages where Christians disagree, without pretending those differences are meaningless.
But we must never allow the debate to eclipse the Savior.
Because one day, the arguments that seemed so important to our pride will stand before the reality of God's holiness.
And the question will not be whether we managed to impress everyone with our theological vocabulary.
The question of eternal significance is whether we belong to Jesus Christ.
So turn to Him while you have breath.
Trust the Gospel.
Walk in repentance.
Live in gratitude.
And tell others about the Savior who receives sinners.
You may not be able to see what God has written in eternity, but you can hear what Jesus is saying to you today: "Come to Me."
